cards.front: What seven activity categories comprise a comprehensive, individualized total exercise program?
cards.back:
A total exercise program includes:
  • Warm-up and stretching activities
  • Endurance training
  • Cool-down and stretching activities
  • Flexibility training
  • Resistance training
  • Neuromotor exercise
  • Recreational activities

cards.front: What is the physiological purpose of a low-intensity dynamic warm-up prior to vigorous exercise?
cards.back: A dynamic warm-up gradually elevates heart rate, breathing, cardiac output, and tissue temperature, preparing the cardiovascular, respiratory, vascular, and neuromuscular systems for efficient and safe functioning during subsequent vigorous exertion.

cards.front: Which types of physical activities serve as the core of an exercise program to develop cardiorespiratory endurance?
cards.back: Activities that involve large muscle groups in continuous, rhythmic motion—such as walking, jogging, running, cycling, swimming, rowing, hiking, and group cardiorespiratory exercise—improve the capacity and efficiency of the cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic systems. Vigorous racquet sports and basketball also provide high aerobic potential.

cards.front: Why is an active cool-down period essential following endurance exercise, and what are the physiological risks of abrupt stopping?
cards.back: An active cool-down (e.g., slow walking) maintains the skeletal muscle pump to prevent venous blood pooling in the lower extremities. Abruptly stopping causes blood to pool in the legs, leading to decreased venous return, dizziness, or fainting (syncope). Furthermore, elevated recovery catecholamine levels combined with abrupt stopping can trigger cardiac dysrhythmias.

cards.front: Why should flexibility exercises be performed slowly, and when during a workout session are tissues most responsive to stretching?
cards.back: Flexibility exercises must be performed slowly because quick, ballistic stretching is dangerous and can trigger muscle spasms or pulls. Musculotendinous structures (muscles, tendons, ligaments, joints) are most compliant and responsive to flexibility training when performed after the endurance conditioning phase when tissue temperature is elevated.

cards.front: What initial load percentage of 1-repetition maximum (1RM) and repetition range are recommended when initiating a resistance training program?
cards.back: Beginners should start with a weight between 40% and 60% of 1RM. Most healthy adults are recommended to perform 8 to 12 repetitions per set for strength and power gains (or up to 15–20 repetitions across 2 to 4 sets for specific endurance/conditioning goals).

cards.front: What is the progressive resistance exercise rule for advancing resistance loads in a training program?
cards.back: When an exerciser can successfully complete 15 repetitions on the first set of an exercise, they are ready to progress to the next higher weight increment.

cards.front: What weekly set volume and exercise selection guidelines apply to resistance training for health and fitness?
cards.back: Performing 2 to 3 sets per exercise, 2 or 3 days per week on non-consecutive days effectively supports strength and weight control goals. In previously untrained individuals, significant strength gains are achieved with just 1 set per day. If time is constrained, set volume should be reduced while maintaining a full-body workout targeting upper body, trunk, and lower body.

cards.front: What is neuromotor exercise (functional training), and what primary functional benefits does it provide?
cards.back: Neuromotor exercise incorporates balance, agility, coordination, gait, proprioceptive training, and core stabilization using multi-joint, multi-planar movements (lunges, lifts, bends). It reactivates muscle groups (such as gluteals and abdominals) inhibited by sedentary behavior, helps prevent falls in older adults, and lowers injury risk in athletes.

cards.front: What five guidelines should be evaluated when selecting recreational activities for a comprehensive health improvement plan?
cards.back:
Recreational activities should be evaluated based on:
  • Skill Competency: Ability to perform with at least a moderate degree of success.
  • Social Opportunity: Opportunities for desired social interaction.
  • Financial Feasibility: Costs within the individual's budget.
  • Long-Term Interest: Variety to sustain continued long-term participation.
  • Safety: Alignment with current age and health status.
